question: Keď kukuričné zrnko v horúcom hrnci zrazu pukne na popcorn, čo ho zvnútra roztrhne?
source_excerpt: water inside the kernel becomes pressurized steam, the hull breaks, and the starch puffs out

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has made popcorn, but few have asked what actually blows the kernel open. The answer is plain water, which feels almost too ordinary, and that is the satisfying 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Water inside the kernel turns to pressurized steam and ruptures the hull; 'voda' is a standard, defensible answer, though strictly it is the steam (vodná para) that bursts the kernel (https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/32131/why-does-popcorn-pop).

explanation: Vo vnútri zrnka je trocha vody, ktorá sa pri ohreve zmení na paru a tlakom roztrhne tvrdú šupku. Preto staré, vysušené zrnká často nepuknú vôbec.

question: Keď zemiaky v pivnici alebo v chladničke dlhšie trpia chladom, zmení sa im chuť. Akými sa stanú?
source_excerpt: Sweetening is variety dependent and can occur at various temperatures (typically below 41°F).

extra.why_interesting: Slovak households traditionally keep potatoes in a cellar, and many people have tasted odd, sweetish potatoes after a cold spell without knowing why. A player can reason from 'cold changes the taste' to a guess, and the starch-to-sugar explanation delivers the payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Cold storage (below ~10 °C / 41°F) causes cold-induced sweetening in potatoes, so they become sweet; see https://idahopotato.com/dr-potato/why-do-potatoes-undergo-cold-induced-sweetening

explanation: Pri chlade sa časť škrobu v zemiakoch mení na cukry, takže zemiaky sladnú. Vďaka tomu aj hranolky z nich pri vyprážaní rýchlejšie zhnednú.

question: Na Lomnickom štíte, vo výške vyše 2600 metrov, začne voda vrieť skôr než dole v nížine. Pri akej teplote približne?

extra.why_interesting: Players know water boils at 100 °C and may vaguely know that altitude lowers that, but they tend to underestimate by how much. Anchoring the fact to a famous Slovak peak, which tourists reach by cable car, makes it tangible. The consequence (eggs cook more slowly at a mountain hut) is the delight.
extra.verification_notes: Lomnický štít is 2634 m; the standard atmosphere gives about 73 kPa there, so water boils at about 91 °C. This is my own calculation, not a cited page, and the Wikipedia link is the source for the peak's height.

explanation: Vo výške je nižší tlak vzduchu, a tak voda vrie už približne pri 91 stupňoch. Preto sa vajíčko na horskej chate varí citeľne dlhšie.

question: Do poriadnej kyslej kapusty sa nepridáva ani kvapka octu, iba soľ. Čo jej teda dáva kyslú chuť?
source_excerpt: the lactic acid formed when the bacteria ferment the carbohydrates in the cabbage leaves

extra.why_interesting: Every Slovak eats kyslá kapusta (kapustnica, segedín) and many assume it is pickled in vinegar like sterilized cucumbers. In fact no vinegar is used: bacteria make the acid themselves. The player can reason toward 'fermentation' from everyday knowledge, and the link to yogurt gives the 'huh, really?' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Sauerkraut's sourness comes from lactic acid produced by lactic acid bacteria fermenting the cabbage's sugars (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauerkraut).

explanation: Baktérie mliečneho kvasenia zjedia cukor z kapusty a premenia ho na kyselinu mliečnu. Je to tá istá kyselina, ktorá robí kyslým jogurt či kyslé mlieko.
